title: The time before
hook: Lucretius: the ages before we were born didn't trouble us, and the ages after won't either

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simmias laughed in a prison cell, and Socrates called philosophy a practice of dying. Your line was practice letting go. What small thing did you set down? Today, a Roman poet who didn't share Plato's view of the soul at all. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

Somewhere there's a photograph of your parents, or grandparents, from before you were born. A wedding, a beach, a kitchen with ugly wallpaper. They're laughing at something. The light is the same light. The world is busy and complete, and you are nowhere in it. Is there anything painful in being absent from it? A Roman poet named Lucretius asked a question very like that, and built a whole argument about death on the answer.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM BEFORE YOU.` → `ANYTHING PAINFUL IN THAT?` → `A POET BUILDS ON IT.`

segments.voice: First, the poet. Lucretius wrote a long poem in Latin verse, On the Nature of Things, to explain the teaching of the Greek philosopher Epicurus. In that teaching, everything, the soul included, is made of tiny particles, and at death they scatter. No one is left to suffer anything. In the third book he says it in a single line: death is nothing to us. Second, the history lesson. He reminds his reader of a terrible time, when Carthage came against Rome from every side and the whole world shook, unsure who would rule land and sea. And we, he says, felt nothing. We weren't there yet. In the same way, when we are no longer here, nothing can touch us, not even if earth and sea and sky are thrown together. Third, the mirror. Later in that book he puts it as a picture. Look back, he says, at the endless ages that passed before we were born. Nature holds that time up to us like a mirror of the time to come after we die. Is there anything frightful in it? Anything gloomy? Isn't it more peaceful than any sleep? Fourth, the honest reply. Not every reader is persuaded. Some answer that what they fear isn't being dead; it's losing this: the people, the morning light, the unfinished things. The mirror doesn't speak to that, and Lucretius's view of the soul is one that other voices in this block reject. But the picture still does something. It makes the vast stretch of nothing before you feel familiar, even restful. That's worth sitting with, whatever you believe comes after.
screen: `DEATH IS NOTHING TO US.` · `WHEN CARTHAGE CAME, WE FELT NOTHING.` · `THE TIME BEFORE IS A MIRROR.` · `NOT EVERY READER IS PERSUADED.` · then, large: `THE TIME BEFORE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Pick a moment from before you were born. A grandparent as a child. A street you know, years before you walked it. A storm nobody remembers now. Let it be vivid: the weather, the sounds, the people busy with their lives. Notice that you're absent from it, and notice how that absence feels. Calm? Strange? Nothing at all? Don't push it toward any conclusion. If thinking about the time after starts to come in, let it sit beside the time before, two quiet rooms. The bell holds the time.
The time before: Lucretius's mirror, the ages before our birth, which never troubled us, held up as a picture of the time after death. Today's word.
Your line: the time before. Today, look at one old photo, or one old place, from before you were born, and notice how it feels to be absent from it. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Some readers of Lucretius use his mirror as a reflection: they recall the long time before their birth and set it beside the time after death, to see whether the fear changes.

original.script: nīl igitur mors est ad nōs
original.say: NEEL IG-ih-toor MORS est ahd NOHS
original.note: Latin, from Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, book three: death, then, is nothing to us.

trapdoor: what you thought: not existing after death is the scariest thought there is.
what it means: Lucretius says we did not exist for ages before birth, and it never troubled us.
what a scholar hears: On the Nature of Things 3.830–842 and 3.972–977, an Epicurean argument resting on a soul made of atoms that scatter.

notes: Lucretius paraphrased (Munro's 1864 translation is public domain but not on the validator's list). The Latin 'nil igitur mors est ad nos' (3.830) is given in the original game only.

Check the paraphrase: Carthaginians coming to battle and the world shaken, uncertain whose rule land and sea would fall under (3.832–837); earth, sea and sky mingled (3.842); the mirror of the time before (3.972–977), 'more untroubled than any sleep'.
